title: Hash Maps: Two Sum
oneLiner: Trade memory for speed: remember what you've seen so far so you never have to look back.
keyTakeaway: A hash map (C#'s Dictionary, Python's dict: a store of key-value pairs that finds the value for a key in about one step) turns "have I seen this value before" from an O(n) re-scan into an O(1) average-case lookup. Any problem shaped like "find a pair / a complement / a duplicate" is a candidate for "store what you've seen in a map as you walk, check it before you add."
explanation: The brute-force way to find two numbers that add up to a target is a nested loop -- for every number, scan every other number -- O(n^2). A hash map does it in one pass: walk the array once, and at each number, ask "have I already seen the complement (target - this number)?" If yes, you're done -- return both indices. If no, remember this number (and its index) in the map and keep going. The map turns "have I seen X" from a re-scan into a lookup, which is what takes this from O(n^2) to O(n). Watch out for using the SAME element twice (nums=[3,3] with target 6 is valid -- two different indices holding equal values -- but you can't pair an element with itself using one index twice).

visualizationSteps.message: Looking for two numbers in [2, 7, 11, 15] that add up to 9. Empty map to start.
nums[0] = 2. Need 7 to reach 9 -- not in the map yet. Add 2 -> index 0 and keep going.
nums[1] = 7. Need 2 to reach 9 -- and 2 is already in the map (from index 0)! Return [0, 1].

complexity.note: One pass with O(1) average lookups, at the cost of storing up to n values -- the classic time-for-space trade versus the O(n²) nested-loop version.
